# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Mildly inappropriate suggestions

**Score:** 64
**Body:** My wife is traveling out of town and it will be just me and the kids. They are 8 and 6 and I want to show them something mildly inappropriate but not wildly. Not sure if I want Action or Comedy but any suggestion would be appreciated.

For some Context we do a Movie night every week and we almost never watch the same film. So we've seen some 200+ movies with my kids.

Edit: Going to bed and the top 3 contenders for far are Tremors, The Mummy, and The Kindergarten Cop. Let's see if anyone can knock those 3 off their spots.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Tremors. It's just a little bit scary and they SWEAR! It's a great "don't tell Mom" movie.
  - Ohhh heck yeah. This is in the running between that and the Mummy so far.
    - The mummy might be too much for the 6 year old. Maybe night at the museum? 
  - Tremors was my families "movie" ever since I was a kid! Its scary but in a fun way, not too inappropriate besides the mild gore/violence. I will stand by this movie forever and ever.
2. I don’t know if you would consider it inappropriate, but I definitely suggest you show them the goonies if you haven’t done so already. Such a fun flick for kids.
3. Who Framed Roger Rabbit is an actual work of genius. Not many movies still hold up as well 40-ish years later.

Watching it as a child and then watching it as an adult is like watching two completely different movies.
4. Coraline, Ghostbusters, Gremlins, Who Framed Roger Rabbit, the Road to El Dorado.
5. The Mummy 99.   Close Encounters of the Third Kind 
6. Jurassic Park 
7. Shaolin Soccer   
Nacho Libre

## 2. Looking for mind-bending Sci-Fi movies with great world-building (like Dune, Blade Runner 2049, or Arrival)

**Score:** 50
**Body:** Hey everyone,I’m looking for some great Sci-Fi movie recommendations. I absolute love films that have a deep, immersive world, a mysterious atmosphere, and a plot that makes you think long after the credits roll.Some of my favorites so far are:Dune (parts 1 & 2) - love the scale and the lore.Blade Runner 2049 - love the cyberpunk aesthetic and slow-burn mystery.Arrival - love the unique concept and the emotional plot twist.I've also seen the classics like The Matrix and Interstellar.What are some other must-watch sci-fi movies that fit this vibe? I prefer modern films (post-2000s) with great visuals, but I'm open to older hidden gems too.Thanks in advance!

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Try
Anaria (2018)

And the series 
the Expanse (2015-2022)
  - Small correction, but the movie is called Aniara. It's hard enough to find by itself imagine with a spelling mistake 😅
2. City of Lost Children 

City of Ember 

Both are dystopian fantasy/sci fi. Neither are as "adult" as what you mentioned but they arent exactly kiddie either. Both have really interesting worlds and are great visual experiences.
3. Dark city
  - Director's cut 
4. I’d go with Annihilation if you haven’t seen it. The atmosphere feels genuinely alien, and I kept thinking about it long after it ended.
5. 5th Element  
Valerian  
Chronicles of Riddick
6. Check out Predestination (2014), Moon (2009), Ad Astra (2019) and Prospect (2018). Predestination and Moon are the more mind bendy type and the other two are more slow world building sci-fi. Ad astra is pretty divisive on here but as long as you go into it knowing it’s more a slow contemplative sci-fi film I think it’s still pretty good.  
7. Edge of Tomorrow 

Pandorum 

Event Horizon 
8. [A Scanner Darkly](https://reelgood.com/movie/a-scanner-darkly-2006) - Explores drugs, the police state, and sanity in a future dystopia.  Based on the story of the same name by Philip K Dick and with an all-star cast (Keanu Reeves, Wynona Ryder, & Robert Downey Jr).

[Myth of Man](https://reelgood.com/movie/myth-of-man-2025) - One of my two favorite films of all time, it’s a masterpiece of visual storytelling.  It's Jamin Winans' ([Ink](https://reelgood.com/movie/ink-2009), [The Frame](https://reelgood.com/movie/the-frame-2014)) newest film.  It follows a young woman in a dangerous steampunk world, who receives a message from her creator that leads her on an epic journey.  It massively over-performs its minuscule budget.  My buddy thought it had a budget 20 times its actual budget.  Be aware that Winans doesn't spell everything out for you and you will have to think about the film to get some of the details.

[Strange Days](https://reelgood.com/movie/strange-days-1995) - Brilliant cyberpunk film from Kathryn Bigelow.  The plot of the film revolves around a black rapper who was shot by two cops, who then attempt to suppress the video of it.

[Mars Express](https://reelgood.com/movie/mars-express-2023) (animated) - A hacker and her android assistant are hired to investigate a murder on Mars.  Really, really good.  

[The Thirteenth Floor](https://reelgood.com/movie/the-thirteenth-floor-1999) - Follows a computer scientist dealing with the murder of his colleague and the launch of a new VR simulation program.  [World on a Wire (1973)](https://reelgood.com/movie/world-on-a-wire-1973) is an older adaptation of the same book (*Simulacron-3* by Daniel Galouye), which is very different, but also brilliant.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. How to analyze a film you did not like?

**Score:** 14
**Body:** For context, lately I have started to write film reviews from the perspective of an amateur, as a hobby. Today, I went to the theater to watch a newly released film with the goal of writing a review about it afterwards. At the end of it, I had the impression that I did not quite like it but I am having a hard time describing what I did not like about it.

The film itself is far away from being bad. From a technical point, it is very well put together. The direction, acting, dialogue, etc. are all good. The problem is that, overall, I did not connect with it. I did not feel that it managed to transmit emotion or something meaningful to last to me as a viewer. I did not quite “care” about it, it felt a little flat. I also do not know if it had a problem from a plot/narration perspective, nor do I have an answer on what could have been changed.

So my question would be, how exactly should we describe and analyze a film that it is not bad and does not have obvious bad elements in it, but rather overall it just did not connect with you as a viewer?

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This sounds obvious, but look up some of Roger Ebert's negative reviews. He does a great job of balancing his criticism with how a movie might appeal to some viewers. Huge part of what makes him the GOAT imo
  - The more you know about film history the easier it is look at any film analytically. You judge a film not only based on your experience but where you believe it stands in the pantheon of other films who did it better and why.
  - man I miss Ebert. Just the other day I was reading his thorough breakdown of Pulp Fiction (not on ebert.com), such an excellent speaker whether I agree with him or not. 
  - Also worth it for some of the best zingers you’ll ever hear about bad movies. His whole review of Battlefield Earth is worth the read, but this quote lives in my head. 

> The director, Roger Christian, has learned from better films that directors sometimes tilt their cameras, but he has not learned why.

https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/battlefield-earth-2000
2. It's too long of a discussion for this forum but there are a couple of ways to approach analysis of film.  
  
The most common method, which most critics use, is adopting the same formula for analyzing literature. You dissect character development, character motivation, dialogue, story structure, meaning and subtext and then see if those elements serviced the story and any internal messaging.

The other method is to understand how the film is made since those decisions ultimately shape what you see on screen. Camera angles, lighting, set design, editing, etc. all play a role and are in service to the vision for the film. When you understand those disciplines, you can then analyze if the choices made were consistent with the tenor, tone, and internal meaning or subtext of the film.

Probably a good approach is to start asking questions. If you feel the film didn't transmit emotion then ask does it need to do that? Was it supposed to do that in a scene? Have you been trained to expect to be stimulated by a film?

I think many expect films to be roller coaster rides where they can passively sit and expect what they are seeing on screen to activate the necessary passages in their brains to deliver these emotional feelings. Not all films are meant to service the viewer and connecting to or enjoying a film is not tied to that concept. Usually it's fairly easy to identify what a film is trying to accomplish and you can then adjust your analysis to fit the type of film you are watching.
  - excellent take, especially the last paragraph. I find myself judging some films based on if it did a good job in conveying what it set out to do, whether it connected with me or not.
  - This reminded me of a quote I was trying to recall that was something along the lines of “art is not always in the service of entertaining the viewer and sometimes there is suffering in understanding.”

I also think there is an obfuscation between judging and analyzing these days. It seems common that people think a judgemental opinion is an important part of critical analyses when it’s not really needed at all.
3. Read Pauline Kael. I own all her books and have read them several times. She very famously hated many of the movies coming out in her time that we now consider “classics,” but the thoughtful way in which she writes her reviews, and often ties her thoughts on the films into other films, the state of the industry, the career of the filmmaker, etc, always makes any of her reviews worth the read, even when she’s trashing a movie you love. She taught me to be more critical of movies I love and more open to discussing movies I don’t care for.
  - I too always admired Kael and collected her books. There was a reddit thread somewhere recently by a hater of Kael, but I always appreciated the fact that even when I disagreed with her verdict she always explained her viewpoint in such a way that I could understand her point of view. She explained her perspective, which I found educational. She made me realize that even when two people seem to agree over a movie, their opinions never match exactly once you delve into the details of those opinions.
4. perfectly normal. i think writing about the cinematography, writing, characters, plots, symbols, comparisons, etc, and then writing about how it made you actually feel, are two different things. both can be included in a review. 

## 2. Watched Out 1 recently and wanted to share some thoughts amd see others thoughts

**Score:** 8
**Body:** After having heard about Out 1 and its status as historically difficult to find/watch (not really the case nowadays) I had it on my list and finally over the last week finished it. Wanted to share some thoughts I had on it, and see what other people thought. 

1. I was surprised in how much I enjoyed watching most of the theater parts as I fully expected them to be hard to sit through but that really wasn't my experience at all. I really loved the energy from Lili's group in the early episodes, and Thomas's group was fun to watch due to how abstracted their rehearsals were. It's the later ones from his group where they started to lose me though, but I really liked the early ones. Could also be I got tired of them as well, but currently don't think so.

2. There was a lot going on with the dynamics of there existing the two theater groups vs the 2 loners (With Colin attempting to join the 13, in his quest to unravel the conspiracy) while Frederique is a loner with little connection to others with the exception of her friendship with Honeymoon and relationdhip with Renaud. Both of them however revert from their temporary collective relationships or companionship by the end with Colin embracing his loner life annoying people for money, while Frederique dies assuming the identity of a lone vigilante. 

3. I knew it connects heavily with May 68, so the idea of the theater groups and the 13 fling apart certainly works with the failure of the protests in 68, and instead a birth or rebirth of individual desires of the actions of the characters. Also think its relevant that both Colin and Frederique focus primarily on ways to get money, tieing in with capitalism and the idea that the individual is all that matters, as well as a rejection of collective action. (I think of anti union policies with this, and how unions and trade organizations have weakened over time).

4. Something that stuck with me was how Thomas's group ended up slowly losing or removing Prometheus from their play. I understood this as the idea that history forgets those who forge ahead over time. Promethus gives Man fire, and initially he would be worshipped or exalted for this. But given time, everyone ends up forgetting this deed, it gets taken for granted, and ultimately forgotten. The case is true for inventiors and scientists. When they first make their big discovery, they end up as heroes, but over time no one thinks about it anymore. The telephone gave Bell massive fame,  and we certainly know his name today, but will that be true in 100 years? Do people think of whoever gave us street lamps that light the night streets, essential medicines that save lives, or household appliances like the potato peeler.

Sorry, if its not very organized as I had a lot to think of from Out 1, and really wanted to share and get other peoples' thoughts

### Top 0 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)


## 3. Someone please explain to me as simple as possible the meaning of talk to her (2002) by Almodovar

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Pedro is my favorite director, I’ve seen almost all his movies, and while I know rape is something he has tackled in several of his movies but this is the first one in which he actually romanticizes it. Before anyone says we are not supposed to feel bad for benigno, Marco tries to get him out, sympathizes with him and also tells him he saved alicia. Side note, in comparison to the rape scene in the skin i live in for most of what I remember, it was totally left ambiguous if Vicente raped the girl or not leaving us some room to sympathize with him, but i really can’t see it here. 

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. If there were a clear-cut meaning to any of this, we wouldn't be talking about it 24 years after the film's release.

Benigno is gentle, attentive, and connected with his own emotions, and yet, he is unable to recognize his patients as fully human when it comes to consent because he is too deeply immersed in what is almost a religious devotion to his work and emotional transfer on his patients. This makes him irrational, or oblivious to both what would generally be considered normal human relationships from an outside perspective (social norms) and to the patient's autonomy.

Should every monster be depicted in a straightforward manner? Should all art aim for vaudeville?

I don't understand why more and more people fall back on moral reductionism to say the most simplistic things imaginable about a piece of media - arguments that could be copy-pasted onto almost any type of art. Any depiction of problematic behavior becomes an analysis of whether the work condones or condemns it. It's really childish, lazy, and pretentious.
2. He raped her. She could not consent. The romanticization is in Benigno's head and hopefully not Almodovar's. Keeping it initially ambiguous, while actually telling us what was happening, was a device Almodovar used to prolong the unfolding of the shock and play on our hope that things that look good are actually pure. Benigno had built a caring relationship in his head while her caregiver which made him outwardly good at it, but he obviously had emotional, relational issues and could not be professional. We are introduced to him as a warm, helpful, caring person but the new information calls his history, and our easy trust in him, into question. Almodovar draws you into his character and leaves you holding the bag filled with the messiness and contradiction of human behavior. It's skillful writing and directing. In many of his movies, rape is somehow brought - he spoken threat of it, human vulnerability to it, actual instances of it, as revenge, as entitlement, as a display of total power, etc. For some reason it's on his mind and he finds it a useful, emotional cinematic device. Maybe Almodovar was raped by someone he trusted. Maybe he raped someone that he somehow feels like he cared for. Maybe he is the product of a rape and has had to grapple with it. I don't know.
3. You’ll have to forgive me that I saw this film a long time ago when it was in the theaters, though this is one of those movies that stayed with me and I think I saw it again shortly after when it came out in video. It was a different world then specially on the issue of mainstream gender and sexual dynamics but the issue you’re bringing up was evident even then. I think there is some moral complexity here. You have to think of the title of the movie, talk to her, it is an invitation that neither of the two characters respond to throughout the film but one that the film exhorts. Benigno and Marco are both examples of flawed masculinity, one is delusional the other one idealizes and cannot really be vulnerable. Benigno actually commits a crime and I think Marco has empathy for him because he makes him realize that he has the possibility to communicate but he squanders it. So many people do great harm thinking they’re actually doing good and he sees that in himself as well. In the end Benigno is like his shadow, he not only shows him what not to do but also confronts him with himself and what if him needs to change about himself. Each man only has their other in their own heads. Benigno doesn’t end well, he pays for his crime and his life is destroyed for it, he confronts his crimes but in the end, Marco still has a chance at a relationship if he can finally communicate and get through the person that is in front of him and not in his head. Thank you for reminding me of this great film I’ll now have to watch again.
4. honestly comparing it to the skin i live in is interesting but they do different things. in talk to her, the whole tragedy is that benigno genuinely believes he is in a mutual relationship. his delusion is complete. the movie doesn't excuse him (he literally goes to prison and dies), it just explores how sad and twisted his delusion is
5. To me, Almodóvar didn't intend to romanticize the rape scene. Instead, he portrayed how Benigno perceived the event. Benigno adored Alicia, and in his mind, he wasn't committing a crime; he believed he was expressing his love for her. Rather than seeing himself as a rapist forcing himself on a defenseless woman, he imagined himself as a tiny, insignificant, harmless man who, in awe and with almost religious reverence, entered the sacred temple of the woman he truly loved.

## 4. Backrooms is a 5-star movie with a 1-star script.

**Score:** 0
**Body:** The true terror isn't in a jumpscare; it's in anticipating one, and Backrooms handles that brilliantly. It genuinely terrified me.

I am personally bothered by analog horror and the uncanny valley, but I still gave it a go. It was gripping right from the start. At one point, the movie had me so hooked I physically couldn't take my eyes off the screen. There were instances where I had to turn the volume down just to brace for an incoming jumpscare. But then... everything falls apart like an unbound rosary.

The movie is shot amazingly. I loved the cinematography and the mise-en-scène. The set designs are a character in their own right. The spaces felt alive. the lights were speaking. The liminal horror just grabs you by the throat.

However the most amazing thing I found in this movie was the sound design. It is truly mesmerizing and elevates an empty frame to entirely new heights. The screams, heavy breathing, sudden beat changes, flickering lights, and typical 90s TV glitches force you to live in that era and feel the dread closing in around you. It made horror in the movie feel sudden yet so anticipated.

Kane Parsons is brilliant as a director. To be a 20-year-old debutant and have this much absolute grip and control over the scenes and actors is astounding. He made legends like Renate Reinsve and Chiwetel Ejiofor act so naturally.

But I guess he wasn't that brilliant as a writer.

First of all, the Backrooms concept serves perfectly as a short film or a web series. To drag it out to a 120-minute feature, you have to tread incredibly carefully. Parsons was amazing in the first act, but he completely lost his grip on the script right from the middle of Act 2 onward.

Unexplained moments, vague scenes, abandoned narratives, underdeveloped characters, incomplete arcs, and a deeply disappointing ending. That is what this movie becomes.

You could cut the lead actors entirely and it would still feel just as scary. In fact, it might even be better, because then the emptiness would feel intentionally ambiguous rather than just incomplete.

Yes, the movie felt much scarier than Obsession (mentioning it since both released around the same time). But Obsession is a far better-written structure. Backrooms is just better at being scary.

Act 3 and the ending bother me the most. Everything just falls flat. Character arcs are rushed, and crucial moments are eaten alive by bad writing. Things suddenly turn illogical and everything feels out of place. Forced drama is inserted out of nowhere. How was Clark surviving in the Backrooms? Who sent Mary the message? What actually happened to Mary? Why was Clark so inconsistent? It feels like the writer started a dozen threads just to abandon them.

And that ending is pure disappointment. It doesn't leave you with a sense of ambiguity, anticipation, or dread. It isn't a cliffhanger. It is just vague, incomplete. It feels like the midpoint of a film, not a climax. Such an amazing, intricate visual structure was completely betrayed by a weak script.

## 5. The Odyssey (review)

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Let me just first say I’m a massive Nolan fan, and I always want his films to do well. I was following the backlash leading up to this release, and I was worried this movie was going to get artificially bad reviews. I was as stoked as could be to see 10’s all over the place, and a 97% on Rotten Tomatoes. Did it live up to the hype? Absolutely not. 

This movie is the definition of style over substance. I don’t care how epic, or profound the original text is supposed to be, it did not translate to the film. 

The movie looks epic as hell. The shots, the locations, set design, costumes, it all looks incredible. The practical effects, the boats, the cyclops, the way the buildings fall down inside the castle walls, all brought to life in a way only Nolan can.

Unfortunately, all the money and set design in the world can’t buy you good story and characters. 

The movie suffers from a lack of conflict, character, and story. A lot of things happen in this movie, but very little of it feels meaningful in any way. We follow one set of characters on an island, as they patiently wait for their king Odysseus to return. I’m not even gonna bother talking about these characters, because they’re all forgettable and nothing interesting takes place on this island until the final act. 

Meanwhile, Odysseus and his crew are just wandering from set piece to set piece, trying to get back home. Bad thing happens, most of them survive it, and then on to the next set piece. You never really get a feel for who Odysseus or any of his crew are, aside from they all want to get back home. There’s not much character or personality amongst any of them, or any conflict between them. They’re just jumping one island to the next, and facing a bunch of monsters who have even less personality than they do. 

Here’s a cyclops! And here’s some giants! And here’s a storm! And here’s a witch! And here’s an undead army! And here’s some sirens! And here’s a sea monster! Epic!!!! 

If this sounds odd on paper, that’s because it is and it doesn’t work any better in the movie. 

The highlight of these adventures is a cyclops in a cave, and it’s quite the sight to behold. Any other director would just make it into a crappy cgi thing, but Nolan pulls off a very impressive practical effect, with (I think) an actual actor playing it in some shots. 

But this scene too, amounts to little more than style over substance. They’re trapped in a cave and trying to get out, aside from the visual, you could replace this cyclops with a couple of orcs from Lord of the Rings and it wouldn’t make much difference. Actually, the orcs would probably be more interesting because they actually talk. 

Which, I actually went back and read this cyclops part from the original text, because I had a feeling there was supposed to be more to it. Turns out this thing actually talks in the original, and I have no idea why Nolan changed it. 

In the original the cyclops taunts them in the cave, belittles them, threatens them, all while eating some of their men right in front of them. It asks Odysseus where their boat is, to which Odysseus is clever, and tells him they shipwrecked, which is a lie. It even asks Odysseus his name and he gives it a fake one. Odysseus and his crew try to bargain with it, and eventually even get it drunk on wine, until it passes out. 

In Nolan’s version it doesn’t even talk to them, and they just stab it in the eye and run out. 

After running from the cave in Nolan’s version, Odysseus turns around in anger and shoots his bow at it. This makes it angry and then it chases their crew. 

In the original, Odysseus turns around and taunts the cyclops, berates it for killing his men, and even gives his real name, as a final taunt. This costs him though, because then the cyclops uses his name to call on the gods to curse him. 

The cyclops curses them in Nolan’s as well, but he sort of just does it. Odysseus fired his bow at it, sure, but that felt more like a understandable outburst of anger, given that it killed some of his men. In the original, Odysseus taunting the cyclops felt like arrogance and a character flaw, that got him in trouble. 

Anyways back to Nolan’s movie. The crew is upset with Odysseus for making the cyclops upset, and getting them cursed. The cyclops is the son of Poseidon and Poseidon controls the ocean, so a lot of rough water ahead. 

Eventually they stop to an island and the crew mutinies Odysseus. They blame him for the curse and want him off the boat. Finally some conflict amongst the crew, something interesting to watch. Except, Odysseus basically just shrugs and says whatever, I’m going hunting. The mutiny is then dropped and never brought up again. 

Like I said, this movie just lacks any real story, character, or conflict. If any other director did this, or it wasn’t based off some ancient text, I’m convinced everyone would just call these scenes pointless filler. 

There’s a nice message in the final act, and it ties back to the beginning of the film and the sacking of Troy. This all amounts to about 5 or 10 minutes in a 3 hour movie, though. 

I respect Nolan for doing things big and never resorting to cgi. Everything is always practical and on epic locations. Even the fact he did The Odyssey, instead of what I feel would be bigger commercially, an Achilles movie, is respectable. Though, Agamemnon’s armor is honestly one of the highlights of this movie, the dude is aura farming like crazy, and I can only imagine how hard an Achilles movie would go by Nolan. 

Rating: 7/10
